prompt.context: Apartment Co is a residential real estate company that owns and operates 10 buildings throughout three different boroughs within New York. The buildings were built between 1975 and 1990 and have been under Apartment Co.'s management since that time. Apartment Co. prides itself on offering affordable, quality apartments for everyday New Yorkers. The only permanent staff in Apartment Co.'s buildings are the doormen. The company operates leasing from their central location in Manhattan, and has contracted with a maintenance service, which will be up for renegotiation soon. Over the last three years, Apartment Co has decided to invest $5M in its infrastructure with the hope of commanding higher apartment rent prices. The company has upgraded many of its apartment unit amenities, including kitchen appliances, bathroom fixtures, and flooring. These improvements have yielded high renter demand as well as increased rent prices. Recently, half of Apartment Co.'s buildings added washers and dryers in the basement; the remaining buildings have no laundry facilities. Even in light of these changes, however, management has not seen the increase in profitability it was hoping for.
prompt.question: Apartment Co has asked your team to assess ways to achieve higher long-term profitability.

clarifying_info.q: What are Apartment Co.'s revenue sources?
clarifying_info.a: The company's sole revenue source is tenant rent; other sources like vending machines and laundry machines are negligible.

clarifying_info.q: How many units are in each building?
How are the buildings distributed across boroughs?
clarifying_info.a: 5 buildings are in Manhattan, 3 in Brooklyn, and 2 in Queens.

clarifying_info.q: Does Apartment Co. own the buildings outright?
clarifying_info.a: All buildings under management are fully owned with no outstanding loans.

clarifying_info.q: How many maintenance staff does the company contract?
clarifying_info.a: The company contracts a staff of 30 to maintain the apartment complexes.

clarifying_info.q: Have there been any recent additions to the real estate portfolio?
clarifying_info.a: No recent additions to the portfolio.
Tenants are mostly young working professionals.

clarifying_info.q: Is the focus on short-term or long-term profitability?
clarifying_info.a: The focus is on long-term profitability; expenditures in the short-term must equate to long-term profitability increases.

framework: Revenue: Analyze occupancy rates, current rent prices, and yearly rent increase rates across Manhattan, Brooklyn, and Queens buildings
Variable Costs: Utilities (electricity, gas, water), amenities upkeep, hourly labor, maintenance contract
Fixed Costs: Property management team salaries, insurance, property taxes
External Factors: Competing rent prices in the market, overall market profitability trends
Long-term lens: Short-term expenditures must translate to sustained profitability improvement

questions.prompt: Review Exhibit 1. What is driving the profitability problem, and what cost category warrants deeper investigation?
questions.guidance: Strong answer identifies that revenue grew from $17M to $20.5M (+21%) but total costs grew faster, from $9.3M to $11.6M (+25%). Key cost increases: Occupancy (Utilities/Insurance) jumped from $1.2M to $2.0M (+67%), and Depreciation jumped from $300K to $1.0M (reflecting the $5M amenity investments). Candidate should flag Occupancy/Utilities as the primary actionable lever since depreciation is a sunk/non-cash item tied to past investment.

steps: Calculate profit margin: 2016=45.3%, 2017=44.5%, 2018=43.4% — declining despite revenue growth
Identify largest cost % increases: Occupancy +67%, Depreciation +233%
Note depreciation is non-cash tied to $5M amenity investment; utilities are the actionable lever
math.answer: Profitability margin is declining. Utilities cost is the primary actionable driver of cost increase (up ~67%); depreciation reflects the past amenity investment.

questions.prompt: Beginning in 2017, management decided to pay for utilities as part of the rental lease agreement to stay competitive. What are some ways Apartment Co. can reduce their utilities expense?
questions.guidance: Candidate should bucket ideas logically. Strong answer covers: Demand side (behavioral) — encourage tenants to turn off AC/lights, rewards for least energy consumption. Supply side (infrastructure) — energy-efficient LED lighting, solar paneling, automatic on/off sensors, more efficient HVAC. By utility type — electricity reduction (LEDs, solar), water reduction (low-flow fixtures), gas reduction (efficient heating). Great candidate also gives creative ideas such as tenant incentive rewards for lowest energy consumption.

questions.prompt: Evaluate Investment Option 1: Installing energy-efficient LED lighting. Calculate the payback period and total savings.
questions.guidance: Candidate should ask for installation cost, number of bulbs, kWh savings per bulb, electricity rate, and bulb lifespan. Then calculate total cost, annual savings, and payback period. Key insight: 2-year payback with 8 years of net savings remaining.

math.setup: Total bulbs = 5,000/building x 10 buildings = 50,000 bulbs. Total installation cost = $30/bulb x 50,000 = $1,500,000. Annual kWh saved = 100 kWh/bulb x 50,000 bulbs = 5,000,000 kWh. Annual savings = 5,000,000 kWh x $0.15/kWh = $750,000. Payback = $1,500,000 / $750,000 = 2 years. Remaining savings years = 10 - 2 = 8 years.
steps: Annual kWh saved: 100 kWh/bulb x 50,000 bulbs = 5,000,000 kWh
Remaining profitable years: 10-year lifespan - 2 years = 8 years of net savings
math.answer: Payback period = 2 years. Net savings over bulb life = 8 years x $750,000 = $6,000,000.

questions.prompt: Evaluate Investment Option 2: Installing solar panels. Calculate the payback period and total savings.
questions.guidance: Candidate should ask for installation cost per sq ft, usable roof area, kWh saved per sq ft, electricity rate, and panel lifespan. Key insight: ~3.3-year payback with ~17 years of net savings remaining. Compare to LED option.

math.setup: Usable roof area per building = 40 ft x 40 ft = 1,600 sq ft. Total sq ft = 1,600 x 10 buildings = 16,000 sq ft. Total installation cost = $200/sq ft x 16,000 sq ft = $3,200,000. Annual kWh saved = 400 kWh/sq ft x 16,000 sq ft = 6,400,000 kWh. Annual savings = 6,400,000 kWh x $0.15/kWh = $960,000. Payback = $3,200,000 / $960,000 = ~3.3 years. Remaining savings years = 20 - 3.3 = ~17 years.
steps: Usable roof area: 40 ft x 40 ft = 1,600 sq ft per building
Total area: 1,600 sq ft x 10 buildings = 16,000 sq ft
Total cost: 16,000 sq ft x $200/sq ft = $3,200,000
Annual kWh saved: 400 kWh/sq ft x 16,000 sq ft = 6,400,000 kWh
Remaining profitable years: 20-year lifespan - 3.3 years ≈ 17 years of net savings
math.answer: Payback period ≈ 3.3 years. Net savings over panel life ≈ 17 years x $960,000 = $16,320,000.

brainstorming.prompt: What are some ways that Apartment Co. can reduce their utilities expense?

categories.name: Demand Side (Behavioral)
ideas: Encourage tenants to turn off AC when not home
Turn off lights in common areas when not in use
Tenant incentive rewards for lowest energy consumption (e.g., gift cards, rent discounts)
Tenant education campaigns on energy conservation

categories.name: Supply Side (Infrastructure — Electricity)
ideas: Install energy-efficient LED lighting throughout buildings
Add automatic on/off sensors for lights in common areas
Upgrade to more energy-efficient HVAC systems

categories.name: Supply Side (Infrastructure — Water)
ideas: Fix leaks proactively through maintenance contracts

categories.name: Supply Side (Infrastructure — Gas)
ideas: Upgrade boilers and heating systems to high-efficiency models
Improve building insulation to reduce heating demand
Install programmable heating controls for common areas

categories.name: Contractual / Operational
ideas: Renegotiate utility contracts for volume discounts
Audit current utility usage to identify waste hotspots

recommendation: Install solar panels: provides greatest annual savings ($960K/year vs. $750K/year), highest total lifetime savings (~$16.3M net), plus potential state/federal tax subsidies and renewable energy credits
Alternative — Install LED lighting: faster payback (2 years vs. 3.3 years), lower upfront cost ($1.5M vs. $3.2M), simpler implementation
Best case — Do both: Apartment Co.'s strong financial position (no outstanding loans, buildings fully owned) allows funding both investments; combined annual savings = $1.71M
Do nothing is defensible only if candidate argues total savings are insufficient relative to risk, opportunity cost of capital, or uncertain energy prices
risks: Volatile energy prices could reduce actual savings below projections
High upfront costs represent significant capital outlay
Opportunity cost: capital could be deployed elsewhere (portfolio expansion, further amenity upgrades)
Tenants may pilfer or damage LED bulbs given their high value
Fickle consumer tastes: if utilities are included, tenants may not value the change
Solar panels subject to government regulation changes or subsidy removal
next_steps: Research and solicit bids from solar panel providers and LED lighting suppliers
Secure licensed subcontractors for installation of panels and/or lighting
Pilot the investment in one building to validate savings projections before full rollout
Monitor energy consumption post-installation to confirm actual vs. projected savings
